head_commit.message:
Refresh recording bounds before leaving Live

Previous used the last polled recording bound, so it could open an older
recording while newer snapshots were stored. Refresh bounds on selection
and use the same cancellation signal for the refresh and snapshot read.

Add regression coverage for stale bounds, cancellation, empty bounds, and
request failures.

QA-021.caption: DashboardServer accepts connections on its own thread and starts bounded connection workers. It shares published JSON with the main receive loop. Live requests use SharedState; history requests read stored data.

main loop: UDP → metrics → JSON
HTTP workers: request → payload

QA-021.title: Build the page into the binary
QA-021.caption: Vite builds dashboard/src into one HTML file. The Makefile converts that output to a byte include. http.hpp places those bytes in kDashboardHtml. The running server needs no separate dashboard file.
QA-021.code:

  → dashboard/dist/index.html
  → build/dashboard_html.inc

QA-021.caption: main.cpp binds a TCP listener from the configured host and port. Listen() sets a backlog of 128. DashboardServer::Start() starts the listener thread and the socket report worker. Connection workers start as requests arrive.

QA-021.caption: Serve() polls the listener with a 200 ms timeout, then calls accept4(). Handle() uses ReadRequest() to read the method, path, query, and headers. Each connection has receive and send timeouts.

poll() → accept4()

help.name: Explain complete-sample latency
help.text:
Complete-sample latency

The sampler takes a timestamp at the start of a thread tick. Latency ends at the last thread packet’s kernel arrival on loopback. It includes thread discovery, /proc reads, encoding, and UDP. It excludes receiver scheduling and collector work. For 500 threads at 10 Hz: median 4.077 ms; p95 4.372 ms.

p95 means 95% of the measured samples completed within that time. This benchmark uses one busy thread and sleeping workers. It does not measure an application with every thread busy.

Close

help.text:
Complete-sample latency

The sampler takes a timestamp at the start of a thread tick. Latency ends at the last thread packet’s kernel arrival on loopback. It includes thread discovery, /proc reads, encoding, and UDP. It excludes receiver scheduling and collector work. For 500 threads at 10 Hz: median 4.077 ms; p95 4.372 ms.

p95 means 95% of the measured samples completed within that time. This benchmark uses one busy thread and sleeping workers. It does not measure an application with every thread busy.

Close

help.name: Explain throughput chart
help.text:
Delivered thread records

One complete sample has one record for each target thread. The measured sample frequency comes from monotonic tick timestamps. 500 threads × 10.000 observed Hz = 5,000.0 records per second.

The sampler uses the configured rate limit. These values do not measure its maximum processing capacity.

Close

help.name: Explain frequency grid
help.text:
Frequency and thread count

Each cell is a measured count/frequency pair. Select a cell to update the cards, selected chart series, and sample interval. Latency uses the median of all samples. CPU uses the mean across 3 trials.

Brighter cells show higher values within the chosen metric. The cell text gives the value without relying on color.

Close

help.name: Explain sample interval share
help.text:
Share of the sample interval

At 10 Hz, sample starts are 100 ms apart. A p95 latency of 4.372 ms uses 4.37% of that interval.

This is wall latency, not CPU use or a maximum sustainable rate. Auxiliary sampling takes additional time after the thread packets are sent.

Close

help.name: Explain sampler CPU
help.text:
Sampler CPU

CPU is execution time from /proc/PID/schedstat divided by monotonic elapsed time. 100% equals one core. The sampler used 4.113% of one core for 500 threads at 10 Hz.

This mean includes default resource and memory-map work. The target workload’s CPU use and the receiver’s CPU use are separate.

Close

help.name: Explain resident memory
help.text:
Resident set size

RSS is the sampler’s resident process memory from /proc/PID/smaps_rollup. Mean 2.03 MiB; maximum observed 2.03 MiB. The driver reads it each second and at the end of each trial.

RSS excludes kernel allocations, target memory, and receiver memory. Short peaks between observations can be missed.

Close

help.name: Explain result statistics
help.text:
How the results are combined

The selected case has 900 complete samples across 3 trials. p50 is the pooled median; p95 uses nearest rank. Trial medians range from 4.066 to 4.092 ms. CPU, RSS, and throughput use the mean across trials.

These are observed values, not confidence intervals or latency guarantees. Low-frequency cases have fewer samples. Raw JSON includes every latency observation and per-trial metrics.

Close

observations.title: Inside the Triangulator dashboard HTTP server
Sampler performance lab — Triangulator
method:
Sampling-loop method and evidence

The timed batch calls FindTarget, Rescan, and TakeSample, then retains each complete thread record. It reuses cached file descriptors. CLOCK_MONOTONIC measures each batch. The loop has no sampling-frequency limit. Percentiles use nearest rank across all 3 repeats.

The continuous loop has different cache and scheduling conditions from the frequency-controlled sampler. The difference between these latency values and UDP delivery latency cannot be attributed to UDP alone. These values do not establish full sampler or collector capacity.

make benchmark-sampling

Recorded sampling-loop baseline · Timed C++ path · Driver

Metric definitions and measurement limits
Complete-sample latency

The sampler writes a real-time timestamp at the start of a thread tick. The receiver uses SO_TIMESTAMPNS_NEW to get each UDP packet’s kernel arrival time. Latency is the latest arrival across all chunks minus that tick timestamp. It includes thread discovery, /proc reads, packet encoding, and loopback UDP. It excludes receiver scheduling, JSON decoding, collector processing, disk writes, and resource or memory-map work after thread delivery. See the Linux timestamp documentation.

Percentiles and repeat variation

p50 is the median of all measured samples for a case. p95 is the nearest-rank 95th percentile of the same observations. Max is the slowest observed sample. The low-frequency cases have fewer observations. A p95 value is a measured tail statistic, not a latency guarantee or confidence interval. The help button next to the table shows the median range across trials for the selected case.

Delivered throughput

Thread records per second equals thread count × observed complete-sample frequency. Frequency uses the elapsed monotonic time between the first and last measured tick. A complete sample contains every expected target thread ID exactly once. This is delivered throughput at 1–10 Hz. The benchmark does not run the sampler without a rate limit, so it cannot establish saturation capacity.

CPU and resident memory

CPU uses the change in /proc/PID/schedstat execution time divided by monotonic elapsed time. 100% means one CPU core. RSS comes from /proc/PID/smaps_rollup, read once per second and at the end. MiB = 1,048,576 bytes. RSS excludes kernel allocations. CPU includes the default resource and memory-map sampling; thread-delivery latency ends before that work.

Scope and environment

These results apply to this host, build, and workload. The host runs a normal desktop; CPUs are not isolated and frequency is not fixed. Most target threads sleep. Results do not establish overhead for 500 CPU-bound threads, rapid thread creation, another host, a remote network, or the collector. Kernel arrival timestamps avoid receiver scheduling delay, but the receiver and desktop can still compete for host resources.

Loss and clock checks

The driver verifies all chunks, packet signatures, session continuity, exact target thread IDs, tick sequence, and tick spacing. It reads one complete sample beyond each measurement window to check the trailing boundary. A missing tick, incomplete sample, warning, or invalid clock measurement aborts the run. Real-time and monotonic elapsed times must agree within 0.1 ms across each run.

Source, build, and evidence

Sampler code is unchanged from the version measured by the sampling-loop benchmark. The benchmark driver adds thread-count coverage, latency timestamps, and checks across measurement boundaries.

QA-021.caption: Get() matches the root path and passes kDashboardHtml to Respond(). The browser receives HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It can now display the dashboard and request JSON.
QA-021.code:
GET /
  → Get()
  → kDashboardHtml
  → Respond(200, …,
      "text/html; charset=utf-8")

QA-021.title: Publish a live JSON snapshot
QA-021.caption: The main loop builds live JSON on an approximately 500 ms refresh cycle. SetLive() exchanges a shared pointer under a mutex. SetMemoryMap() publishes a layout when its version changes.
QA-021.code:
DumpJson(live)
  → shared_ptr<const string>
  → state.SetLive(…)

Layout changed? SetMemoryMap(…)

nodes.text: Main receive loopIngest → MonitorPublish JSON every ~0.5 s

QA-021.title: Fetch JSON and update the charts
QA-021.caption: The dashboard fetches /api/live, then schedules the next refresh after 1 second. Get() reads SharedState::Live(). It sends the saved JSON without querying SQLite. Browser JavaScript updates the charts.
QA-021.code:
fetch("/api/live")
  → state_.Live()
  → Respond(200, JSON,
      "application/json")
  → browser renders metrics

QA-021.title: Query stored thread summaries
QA-021.caption: The thread history request supplies a session, TID, and time range. History() validates these values and reads SQLite day files. The response contains rows, limit, and truncated fields.
QA-021.code:
GET /api/history?session=…
  &tid=…&start=…&end=…
  → History(data_dir_, …)
  → JSON: rows, limit, truncated
// maximum: 2,000 rows

QA-021.title: Send bytes, then close
QA-021.caption: Respond() adds HTTP/1.0 headers and sends until all bytes are written or send() fails. FileDescriptor closes the connection when its scope ends. Serve() then waits for the next connection.
QA-021.code:
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: …
Cache-Control: no-store

send(…, MSG_NOSIGNAL) → close

help.name: Explain complete-sample latency
help.text:
Complete-sample latency

The sampler takes a timestamp at the start of a thread tick. Latency ends at the last thread packet’s kernel arrival on loopback. It includes thread discovery, /proc reads, encoding, and UDP. It excludes receiver scheduling and collector work. For 500 threads at 10 Hz: median 4.077 ms; p95 4.372 ms.

p95 means 95% of the measured samples completed within that time. This benchmark uses one busy thread and sleeping workers. It does not measure an application with every thread busy.

Close

help.name: Explain latency chart
help.text:
Complete-sample latency

The sampler takes a timestamp at the start of a thread tick. Latency ends at the last thread packet’s kernel arrival on loopback. It includes thread discovery, /proc reads, encoding, and UDP. It excludes receiver scheduling and collector work. For 500 threads at 10 Hz: median 4.077 ms; p95 4.372 ms.

p95 means 95% of the measured samples completed within that time. This benchmark uses one busy thread and sleeping workers. It does not measure an application with every thread busy.

Close

help.name: Explain throughput chart
help.text:
Delivered thread records

One complete sample has one record for each target thread. The measured sample frequency comes from monotonic tick timestamps. 500 threads × 10.000 observed Hz = 5,000.0 records per second.

The sampler uses the configured rate limit. These values do not measure its maximum processing capacity.

Close

help.name: Explain frequency grid
help.text:
Frequency and thread count

Each cell is a measured count/frequency pair. Select a cell to update the cards, selected chart series, and sample interval. Latency uses the median of all samples. CPU uses the mean across 3 trials.

Brighter cells show higher values within the chosen metric. The cell text gives the value without relying on color.

Close

help.name: Explain sample interval share
help.text:
Share of the sample interval

At 10 Hz, sample starts are 100 ms apart. A p95 latency of 4.372 ms uses 4.37% of that interval.

This is wall latency, not CPU use or a maximum sustainable rate. Auxiliary sampling takes additional time after the thread packets are sent.

Close

help.name: Explain sampler CPU
help.text:
Sampler CPU

CPU is execution time from /proc/PID/schedstat divided by monotonic elapsed time. 100% equals one core. The sampler used 4.113% of one core for 500 threads at 10 Hz.

This mean includes default resource and memory-map work. The target workload’s CPU use and the receiver’s CPU use are separate.

Close

help.name: Explain resident memory
help.text:
Resident set size

RSS is the sampler’s resident process memory from /proc/PID/smaps_rollup. Mean 2.03 MiB; maximum observed 2.03 MiB. The driver reads it each second and at the end of each trial.

RSS excludes kernel allocations, target memory, and receiver memory. Short peaks between observations can be missed.

Close

help.name: Explain result statistics
help.text:
How the results are combined

The selected case has 900 complete samples across 3 trials. p50 is the pooled median; p95 uses nearest rank. Trial medians range from 4.066 to 4.092 ms. CPU, RSS, and throughput use the mean across trials.

These are observed values, not confidence intervals or latency guarantees. Low-frequency cases have fewer samples. Raw JSON includes every latency observation and per-trial metrics.

Close

STEP 1 OF 9
Separate workers, one collector

DashboardServer accepts connections on its own thread and starts bounded connection workers. It shares published JSON with the main receive loop. Live requests use SharedState; history requests read stored data.

main loop: UDP → metrics → JSON
HTTP workers: request → payload

Why the threads are separate

The main loop receives UDP samples. The HTTP workers can wait on a browser or a history query without doing that work in the receive loop.

A mutex protects the snapshot pointer exchange. Each HTTP worker retains an immutable JSON string and sends it after the lock is released.

Connection limits

Serve() starts up to 64 connection workers. A slow request uses one worker. The listener backlog is 128. Reading the complete request has a 5-second total deadline. Sending the response has a separate 5-second total deadline. Excess connections receive HTTP 503.

Responses use HTTP/1.0. The connection closes after each request. The C++ server uses plain HTTP and has no TLS handshake.

observations.text:
×
Largest unmapped gap

Selected bar · complete current layout

The longest uncovered address interval inside the selected bar.

Example. Two mappings separated by 64 KiB have a 64 KiB gap.

Compare with the total not mapped inside the bar. Unknown coverage is shown separately from unmapped space.

Limits. An unmapped gap is not an allocator free block. Incomplete, stale, or historical layouts cannot supply this value.

Source. Computed from `/proc/PID/maps`

observations.name: help heapend
observations.text:
×
Heap mapping end

Process · page-aligned heap boundary

The upper address of the heap mapping, plotted as a byte offset from the first available sample in this chart.

Example. An offset of +64 KiB means the mapping end moved up by 64 KiB.

Read steps as sampled changes. The rate uses the measured sample times.

Limits. This is not the exact program break. Missing samples leave gaps. History resets when the target or sampler session changes.

Source. End address of the [heap] line of `/proc/PID/maps`

observations.name: help stackstart
observations.text:

Main stack start

Main thread · lower mapping boundary

The lower address of the main stack mapping, plotted as an offset from the first available sample in this chart.

Example. An offset of −64 KiB means the mapping grew down by 64 KiB.

A downward step means a lower mapping start. Read mapped size in the selected stack facts.

Limits. The mapping boundary does not measure stack depth. Missing samples leave gaps.

Resident anonymous

Process · RssAnon over time

Anonymous memory currently in RAM: heap, arenas, thread stacks, and private mmap memory.

A sustained slope, shown per minute, is a better growth signal than virtual size.

Limits. Swapped anonymous pages leave this total. The chart covers only the time this page was open.

observations.name: help heap
observations.text:
×
Heap size

Process · [heap] mapping over time

The size of the brk heap. It grows up when the allocator calls brk.

A sustained rise, together with RSS growth, can indicate allocation growth.

Limits. Many allocators also use mmap arenas. Size change uses samples collected while this page was open and shows their measured interval. It is not an exact program-break movement.

Source. The [heap] line of `/proc/PID/maps`
The size of the [heap] line of `/proc/PID/maps` (end address minus start address) in each memory sample. Check it yourself: `grep heap /proc/PID/maps`.

observations.name: help threadstacks
observations.text:
×
Thread stacks

Other threads · reserved mappings and residency

Common pthread stacks reserve a fixed address range. The number of resident pages can change inside that range.

A fixed mapping size does not mean fixed memory use. The main stack boundary chart covers only the main thread.

Limits. Other runtimes can manage stacks differently. Residency does not measure current stack depth.

Source. Anonymous lines of `/proc/PID/maps`
The dashboard does not measure the residency of each thread stack. Thread stacks appear as anonymous lines in `/proc/PID/maps`, usually with a guard page below them.

observations.name: help threadstacks
observations.text:
×
Thread stacks

Other threads · reserved mappings and residency

Common pthread stacks reserve a fixed address range. The number of resident pages can change inside that range.

A fixed mapping size does not mean fixed memory use. The main stack boundary chart covers only the main thread.

Limits. Other runtimes can manage stacks differently. Residency does not measure current stack depth.

Source. Anonymous lines of `/proc/PID/maps`
The dashboard does not measure the residency of each thread stack. Thread stacks appear as anonymous lines in `/proc/PID/maps`, usually with a guard page below them.

Anonymous memory currently in RAM: heap, arenas, thread stacks, and private mmap memory.

observations.name: help heap
observations.text:
×
Heap size

Process · [heap] mapping over time

The size of the brk heap. It grows up when the allocator calls brk.

A sustained rise, together with RSS growth, can indicate allocation growth.

Limits. Many allocators also use mmap arenas. Size change uses samples collected while this page was open and shows their measured interval. It is not an exact program-break movement.

Source. The [heap] line of `/proc/PID/maps`
The size of the [heap] line of `/proc/PID/maps` (end address minus start address) in each memory sample. Check it yourself: `grep heap /proc/PID/maps`.

observations.name: help threadstacks
observations.text:
×
Thread stacks

Other threads · reserved mappings and residency

Common pthread stacks reserve a fixed address range. The number of resident pages can change inside that range.

A fixed mapping size does not mean fixed memory use. The main stack boundary chart covers only the main thread.

Limits. Other runtimes can manage stacks differently. Residency does not measure current stack depth.

Source. Anonymous lines of `/proc/PID/maps`
The dashboard does not measure the residency of each thread stack. Thread stacks appear as anonymous lines in `/proc/PID/maps`, usually with a guard page below them.

observations.name: help threadstacks
observations.text:
×
Thread stacks

Other threads · reserved mappings and residency

Common pthread stacks reserve a fixed address range. The number of resident pages can change inside that range.

A fixed mapping size does not mean fixed memory use. The main stack boundary chart covers only the main thread.

Limits. Other runtimes can manage stacks differently. Residency does not measure current stack depth.

Source. Anonymous lines of `/proc/PID/maps`
The dashboard does not measure the residency of each thread stack. Thread stacks appear as anonymous lines in `/proc/PID/maps`, usually with a guard page below them.

fixtureInputs.pidBoundary: An extra session 100/PID 8 row at last-6 has RSS null, fd_open=88 and retransmission delta 100000. It lies between PID 7 rows at last-10 and last-5.
fixtureInputs.futureRow: A session 100/PID 8 row at last+1 has RSS=999999999999 and retransmission delta 100000; recorded reads exclude it.
fixtureInputs.rangeCounts: Each PID 7 row has retransmission delta 1. The displayed recorded counter totals 48; RSS, open-files and retransmission charts each have 48 points in both variants.
fixtureInputs.earlierPeriods: A second recording and 48-row growth run are shifted exactly 3600 seconds earlier. Load earlier preserves the first row and adds the older row. Both selected assessments agree.
fixtureInputs.fixtureRevision: Recipe adapted from tests/replay_fixture.py and tests/prove_replay.mjs at c16a55383c4bc6a219c270aa4f7cf9b55c97e45a; owned adaptation files are common.mjs, seed.py, run.mjs, extended.mjs, memory-final.mjs and last.mjs.

help.text:
×
CPU

One core · percentage

CPU time used, as a percentage of one CPU core.

Example. 50% means 0.5 seconds of CPU time per elapsed second.

Compare CPU use with run delay. Process CPU sums all reported threads and can exceed 100%.

Limits. A high value can be normal for a busy worker. CPU use alone does not establish a problem.

Source. `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat`: utime + stime
Each sample, the sampler reads `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat` for every thread. Fields 14 (utime) and 15 (stime) are the CPU time the thread used in user and kernel mode, in clock ticks (usually 100 per second). The collector divides the change between two samples by the time between them. Process CPU sums the threads. `top -H -p PID` reads the same counters.

CPU

One core · percentage

CPU time used, as a percentage of one CPU core.

Example. 50% means 0.5 seconds of CPU time per elapsed second.

Compare CPU use with run delay. Process CPU sums all reported threads and can exceed 100%.

Limits. A high value can be normal for a busy worker. CPU use alone does not establish a problem.

Source. `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat`: utime + stime
Each sample, the sampler reads `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat` for every thread. Fields 14 (utime) and 15 (stime) are the CPU time the thread used in user and kernel mode, in clock ticks (usually 100 per second). The collector divides the change between two samples by the time between them. Process CPU sums the threads. `top -H -p PID` reads the same counters.

observations.name: hover source delay
observations.text:
×
Run delay

Elapsed time · percentage

Time a thread was ready to run but waited for a CPU.

Example. 12% means 120 ms waiting per elapsed second.

Persistent delay can indicate competition for CPU time. Compare CPU use, cgroup CPU pressure, and quota throttling.

Limits. Sleep and futex wait are separate measurements. Run delay alone does not identify a cause.

Source. `/proc/PID/task/TID/schedstat`: second number
Each sample, the sampler reads `/proc/PID/task/TID/schedstat`. Its second number is the total time, in nanoseconds, that the thread was ready to run but waited for a CPU. The collector divides the change between two samples by the time between them. With `status_fallback = true` in sampler.toml, the sampler reads `status` instead, and run delay is not available. Check it yourself: `cat /proc/PID/task/TID/schedstat`.

observations.name: hover source states
observations.text:
×
Thread states

Sampled scheduler state and wait channel

A sampled classification of what a thread is doing or waiting for.

Example. Futex wait can indicate a lock, condition variable, or timed idle wait.

Running is blue and Sleep is green. State colors match across the map, state mix, charts, and wait-channel bars. Other and No access have separate gray colors. Read the state together with CPU use, run delay, and the kernel wait channel. Select a state to filter the table.

Limits. Samples can miss brief transitions. A wait state does not establish that the application is unhealthy.

Source. `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat` field 3, and `wchan`
Field 3 of `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat` is the scheduler state letter. For a sleeping thread, `/proc/PID/task/TID/wchan` names the kernel function it waits in. The collector maps R to Running, D to Kernel wait, and T or t to Stopped. Otherwise it matches the wait channel: futex; epoll, poll, or select; socket functions; pipe or eventfd; and nanosleep. An empty wait channel is No access. Check it yourself: `ps -L -o tid,stat,wchan:32,comm -p PID`.

observations.text:
METRIC GUIDE
Close ×
Pressure stalls (PSI)

Displayed host or cgroup · time share

Pressure stall information measures time tasks waited for CPU, memory, or I/O.

Example

Some: at least one task waited. Full: all non-idle tasks waited at once.

How to read it

Table values cover the latest resource interval; chart points show interval peaks. The first sample can use the kernel avg10 average. Assessment checks CPU some at 20%, memory some at 5% or full at 2%, and I/O some at 10% or full at 5%.

Measurement limits

The target cgroup can contain other processes. Host values cover the entire host. Host CPU full is not a useful stall measure.

Source

Host values come from /proc/pressure/cpu, memory, and io. Cgroup values come from cpu.pressure, memory.pressure, and io.pressure in the target cgroup directory under /sys/fs/cgroup, found from /proc/PID/cgroup. Interval values use the change of the cumulative total= stall time; the first sample uses avg10. Check it yourself: cat /proc/pressure/cpu.

Network drops

Target network namespace

Selected counters for dropped packets or connections in the target network namespace.

Example

Example: 0/s, 20, and 500 mean no events in the latest interval, 20 in the selected range, and a cumulative count of 500.

How to read it

Rate (/s) is events per second over the latest sample interval. In range adds events from available samples in the selected time range. Total is the kernel counter and can include events before monitoring started. Read each counter definition.

Measurement limits

Other processes can contribute. Counter resets, gaps, and partial coverage can limit comparisons.

Source

With each resource sample, the sampler reads counters from /proc/PID/net/netstat (TcpExt), /proc/PID/net/snmp (Tcp and Udp), /proc/PID/net/snmp6 (Udp6, added to Udp), and /proc/PID/net/dev (every interface except lo). These files describe the network namespace of the target. Each counter topic names its line. Check it yourself: cat /proc/PID/net/netstat.

failures.text:
×
Run delay

Elapsed time · percentage

Time a thread was ready to run but waited for a CPU.

Example. 12% means 120 ms waiting per elapsed second.

Persistent delay can indicate competition for CPU time. Compare CPU use, cgroup CPU pressure, and quota throttling.

Limits. Sleep and futex wait are separate measurements. Run delay alone does not identify a cause.

Source. `/proc/PID/task/TID/schedstat`: second number
Each sample, the sampler reads `/proc/PID/task/TID/schedstat`. Its second number is the total time, in nanoseconds, that the thread was ready to run but waited for a CPU. The collector divides the change between two samples by the time between them. With `status_fallback = true` in sampler.toml, the sampler reads `status` instead, and run delay is not available. Check it yourself: `cat /proc/PID/task/TID/schedstat`.

failures.name: hover code formatting states
failures.text:
×
Thread states

Sampled scheduler state and wait channel

A sampled classification of what a thread is doing or waiting for.

Example. Futex wait can indicate a lock, condition variable, or timed idle wait.

Running is blue and Sleep is green. State colors match across the map, state mix, charts, and wait-channel bars. Other and No access have separate gray colors. Read the state together with CPU use, run delay, and the kernel wait channel. Select a state to filter the table.

Limits. Samples can miss brief transitions. A wait state does not establish that the application is unhealthy.

Source. `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat` field 3, and `wchan`
Field 3 of `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat` is the scheduler state letter. For a sleeping thread, `/proc/PID/task/TID/wchan` names the kernel function it waits in. The collector maps R to Running, D to Kernel wait, and T or t to Stopped. Otherwise it matches the wait channel: futex; epoll, poll, or select; socket functions; pipe or eventfd; and nanosleep. An empty wait channel is No access. Check it yourself: `ps -L -o tid,stat,wchan:32,comm -p PID`.

observations.name: source guide exitreason
observations.title: Last process exit
observations.text:
METRIC GUIDE
Close ×
Last process exit

Ended target process · kernel log and exit status

Why the most recent target process ended: from the kernel log messages that name the process or one of its threads, else from its exit status.

Example

"Segmentation fault" means the kernel logged a memory fault. "Crashed: SIGABRT" means the process called abort(), which the kernel does not log.

How to read it

Read the reason first, then the exit status and the kernel messages. The time is when the sampler noticed the exit, within one sample interval. The card is open while the ended process is the one the page shows. Once another process is the target, it folds to one line with the reason, the time and the number of exits since the collector started; open it for the details.

Measurement limits

The kernel logs only the faults it handles and the out-of-memory killer, and reading the log needs kernel.dmesg_restrict = 0. The exit status names the signal or exit code without that, on Linux 6.15 and later, or when the sampler sees the process as a zombie. "No kernel crash message" means neither was found, so it does not prove the process did not crash. The card shows the latest exit since the collector started.

Source

The sampler reads new kernel log records from /dev/kmsg that name the target PID or one of its threads, such as a segfault or an OOM kill. If none names it, the reason comes from the exit status (see Exit status). Reading /dev/kmsg can need CAP_SYSLOG when kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1. Check it yourself: dmesg | grep PID.

observations.name: source guide exitstatus
observations.title: Exit status
observations.text:
METRIC GUIDE
Close ×
Exit status

Ended target process · waitpid status

The signal or exit code that ended the process, as its parent would see it from waitpid().

Example

"SIGSEGV (signal 11), core dumped" is a crash. "exit code 3" means the process called exit(3).

How to read it

A crash signal (SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, SIGBUS, SIGFPE, SIGILL, SIGTRAP, SIGSYS) is a fault in the process. SIGKILL, SIGTERM and SIGINT usually come from another process. Exit code 0 is a normal exit.

Measurement limits

The sampler is not the parent. It reads the status through a pidfd on Linux 6.15 and later, which needs no privileges, or from /proc while the process is a zombie. On older kernels the parent often reaps the process first, and the status is not available. SIGKILL from the out-of-memory killer looks like kill -9 unless the kernel log is readable.

Source

The sampler opens a pidfd for the target with pidfd_open when it finds it. On Linux 6.15 and later, the PIDFD_GET_INFO ioctl returns the exit status after the parent reaps the process. While the process is a zombie, the sampler can also read field 52 (exit_code) of /proc/PID/stat.

cards:
×
Past assessments

Recordings · checked period

What the Assessment found in the past. The dashboard reads recorded views of the process and applies the same fixed rules as the Assessment card to each one.

Example. When the page opens, up to 120 recordings of the last 15 minutes are checked, one every ~8 s. “worker-3 is saturating a core” seen from 14:02:10 to 14:05:40 in 25 checked recordings is one row, and one red mark on the timeline.

Rows are newest first. Each shows the worst level it reached, when it was first and last seen, its type, and how many checked recordings had it. Select a row to move the whole dashboard to its worst moment: the Assessment card then shows the same finding and the row shows its detail. Scroll to the end of the list, select Load earlier, or release the timeline at its left end to check an earlier period; each is twice as long as the one before, up to 6 hours. While live, newer recordings are added every 15 seconds.

Limits. Each period checks up to 120 recordings, so older periods are checked more coarsely: a problem that starts and ends between two of them is not listed, and its first and last times are accurate only to the step. Recording gaps end a row. Each recording is judged on its own: rules that need trends kept in a live tab (thread growth, thread churn, long futex waits) and the watch rule with no thread do not run. Resident memory growth uses the stored resource samples before each recording, combined into coarser steps for long periods. The main-stack rule runs only while the recording’s memory map is still the newest one. Nothing is stored: a reload checks again. Every checked recording is downloaded, about 330 KB each with 1,000 threads.

Source. Recordings from `/api/replay`, checked in this page

Select a row to move the whole dashboard to its worst moment: the Assessment card then shows the same finding and the row shows its detail. Scroll to the end of the list, select Load earlier, or release the timeline at its left end to check an earlier period; each is twice as long as the one before, up to 6 hours. While live, newer recordings are added every 15 seconds.

Limits. Each period checks up to 120 recordings, so older periods are checked more coarsely: a problem that starts and ends between two of them is not listed, and its first and last times are accurate only to the step. Recording gaps end a row. Each recording is judged on its own: rules that need trends kept in a live tab (thread growth, thread churn, long futex waits) and the watch rule with no thread do not run. Resident memory growth uses the stored resource samples before each recording, combined into coarser steps for long periods. The main-stack rule runs only while the recording’s memory map is still the newest one. Nothing is stored: a reload checks again. Every checked recording is downloaded, about 330 KB each with 1,000 threads.

Active threads

Threads · preceding ~10 seconds

Threads with recent CPU use, context switches, or I/O. Blocked or stopped threads are not treated as idle.

A thread is active when, in the preceding ~10 seconds, it used CPU (`stat` utime + stime), was put on a CPU (`schedstat`), read or wrote (`io` rchar, wchar), had a major fault (`stat` majflt), or was sampled running, in kernel wait, or stopped. How often the scheduler switches execution to or from the observed threads.

observations.name: desktop refresh hover churn Thread churn
cards:
×
Thread churn

Process · preceding minute

Threads seen starting or ending during the last minute. This is a lower bound: a thread is counted only if a sample catches it alive.

Example. +4 / −2 means four starts and two ends were seen. +0 / −0 means none were seen, not that none happened.

Compare sustained churn with worker-pool behavior and process restarts. If the process creates short-lived threads, expect the real number to be higher, often far higher.

Limits. A thread that starts and exits between two samples is never seen, and the kernel offers no unprivileged count of threads created. At 2 samples/s, a thread living 10 ms is seen about 2% of the time. Raise the sample rate, or count thread creations inside the application.

Source. Thread IDs in `/proc/PID/task`, compared between updates
Each sample, the sampler lists `/proc/PID/task`, which has one entry per live thread. This page compares the thread IDs of consecutive live updates: a new ID counts as a start and a missing ID as an end. The kernel keeps no count of created threads that an unprivileged reader can see.

Thread states

Sampled scheduler state and wait channel

A sampled classification of what a thread is doing or waiting for.

Example. Futex wait can indicate a lock, condition variable, or timed idle wait.

An empty wait channel is No access. Check it yourself: `ps -L -o tid,stat,wchan:32,comm -p PID`.

One core · percentage

Run delay

Elapsed time · percentage

Time a thread was ready to run but waited for a CPU.

Example. 12% means 120 ms waiting per elapsed second.

Persistent delay can indicate competition for CPU time. Compare CPU use, cgroup CPU pressure, and quota throttling.

Limits. Sleep and futex wait are separate measurements. Run delay alone does not identify a cause.

Source. `/proc/PID/task/TID/schedstat`: second number
Each sample, the sampler reads `/proc/PID/task/TID/schedstat`. Its second number is the total time, in nanoseconds, that the thread was ready to run but waited for a CPU. Displayed host or cgroup · time share

Pressure stall information measures time tasks waited for CPU, memory, or I/O.

observations.name: desktop refresh hover socketio Socket I/O & message processing
cards:
×
Socket I/O & message processing

Optional observer · target process

Traffic measured by observed socket operations, with optional application completion counts.

The cards and chart cover the whole process. Thread and socket-kind filters affect the breakdown only, which includes retired threads.

Limits. Received/sent bytes exclude peeks, failed operations, and UDP. A receive call can contain part of a message or many messages.

Source. Optional eBPF observer: kernel tracepoints and a uprobe
The optional eBPF socket observer attaches to the kernel tracepoints sock_recv_length and sock_send_length. It counts, for each thread of the target, the bytes of successful socket receives and sends in kernel maps, and reports them to the collector once a second. Message counts come from a uprobe on the application marker function. Loading it needs privileges. The collector shows the observer that last reported the selected target's PID from the same sampler host. After a collector restart, it shows the stored observations of that PID until an observer reports, unless another target has the same PID.

observations.name: desktop refresh hover watches Watched threads
cards:
×
Watch rules

Collector · thread name prefixes

Rules that say threads whose name starts with a prefix should wake at least every N milliseconds, as workers that wait with a timeout do. The Assessment flags a matching thread that stops waking (a possible deadlock, or a wait with no timeout) or keeps a core busy (a possible infinite loop).

Example. "worker-" every 500 ms watches worker-1, worker-2 and so on. A thread that has not run for much longer than 500 ms is then reported.

Add one rule per group of threads that should keep waking. When several prefixes match, the longest one is used, so "worker-" and "worker-io" can have different intervals. Check Matching threads now before you save.

Limits. The collector only reports when each thread last ran. A thread with a long wait by design, or a name that no rule matches, is not watched. A rule does not start or stop anything.

Source. [[watch]] in collector.toml, or `data_dir/watch-rules.json`
The collector reads the [[watch]] tables of collector.toml when it starts. Rules saved from this page replace them for the selected target until Reset. Target files are in `data_dir/watch-rules/`; the default target that keeps `data_dir/replay` keeps `data_dir/watch-rules.json`. This page reads the rules in force from `/api/watches`.

observations.name: desktop refresh hover watchprefix Thread name prefix
cards:
×
Thread name prefix

One rule · UTF-8 bytes

The start of the thread names the rule applies to. A rule matches every thread whose name begins with these characters, with the same upper and lower case.

Example. "worker-" matches worker-1 and worker-io but not Worker-1 or my-worker-1.

Use 1 to 15 bytes. Linux thread names are at most 15 bytes, so a longer prefix could never match. Each prefix may appear once. The count next to it shows at once whether the prefix is right.

Limits. Spaces count, so a trailing space must match the name. Characters outside ASCII use more than one byte. The tab checks the rules again on save, and the collector has the final say.

observations.name: desktop refresh hover watchwake Wakes at least every (ms)
cards:
×
Wakes at least every (ms)

One rule · milliseconds

The longest time a matching thread may go without running before it counts as stuck. Workers that wait with a timeout wake at least this often.

Example. 500 means the thread should run at least twice a second.

Use a whole number from 10 to 3,600,000 (one hour). Choose a value above the thread's wait timeout, plus some margin for a busy host. A value close to the sample interval is noisy.

Limits. A thread that waits without a timeout will never meet a small value. That is what the rule is meant to show, but it can also be a thread that is idle by design.

How many threads of the monitored process have a name that starts with this prefix right now, counting each thread under the longest matching prefix, as the collector does. A few names follow the count.

It updates while you type and as threads start and stop, before anything is saved. 0 usually means a typo, wrong case, or threads that do not exist yet. A note shows threads that match this prefix but use a longer one.

How to read this page

Dashboard guide

Read the scope, unit, time interval, and data status before interpreting a metric.

Read Assessment first, then the key measurements and charts. Open Timeline below the charts to inspect recordings. Use Theme in the header to select System, Light, or Dark. Pause over a label or value for 3 seconds. Focus a Help label for the same delay, or press Enter or Space on it for immediate help. Tap a Help label for immediate help. Open metric help, then select Open metric guide for an example, measurement limits, chart data, and related topics. Use Open page guide for every topic. Show help on hover controls pointer help; keyboard and touch help remain available. Select a ▸ heading to open or close its panel. The page remembers that choice in this browser. Monitor health, Address space & zoom, and Network stack drops open by themselves when the Assessment has a warning of their kind, until you choose.

Limits. A single metric does not establish a cause. Missing data is not zero.

Source. `/proc` and `/sys/fs/cgroup` → sampler → collector → this page
The sampler runs on the target host as the target user. It reads `/proc` and `/sys/fs/cgroup` files and sends the raw counters over UDP. The collector turns counters into rates, stores history, and serves this page through `/api/…` endpoints. This page computes load, assessments, and findings. The optional eBPF observer adds socket bytes and messages. The Source section of each topic names its file.

Active threads

Threads · preceding ~10 seconds

Threads with recent CPU use, context switches, or I/O. Blocked or stopped threads are not treated as idle.

Example. An idle worker can still be waiting normally for its next task.

Active, Idle, and All change which threads are listed. Clear filters to restore the default view.

Limits. Idle does not mean exited. A sampling gap is not evidence of inactivity.

Source. Thread counters in `/proc/PID/task/TID/`
A thread is active when, in the preceding ~10 seconds, it used CPU (`stat` utime + stime), was put on a CPU (`schedstat`), read or wrote (`io` rchar, wchar), had a major fault (`stat` majflt), or was sampled running, in kernel wait, or stopped. The collector computes the rates; this page applies the rule.

This browser tab · Targets overview

help.fleet:
METRIC GUIDE
Close ×
Targets overview

Every target of this collector · latest live view

The first page: one tile per monitored process, with its current assessment. The counts above the tiles total every target by level, including targets that a search or status hides.

Example

Critical 1 · Healthy 3 means one process needs attention now and three show no problem.

How to read it

Tiles are sorted worst first, then by host and target ID. Select a tile, or open it in a new tab, to see that process's dashboard; All targets on the dashboard returns here. The tab title starts with the number of targets at warning or worse. The page refreshes every 5 seconds while it is visible.

Measurement limits

Tiles do not run trend rules or memory-map layout rules. Each refresh reads the latest live view of every target, so a large number of targets costs more network traffic than one dashboard.

Source

The page reads the target list, then the latest live view of each target, at most 4 at a time, every 5 seconds.

help.fleet-tile:
METRIC GUIDE
Close ×
Target tile

One target · latest live view

The process name, host and target ID identify the target. A long name ends with an ellipsis; point at it to see the full name. One dot shows the assessment of its latest live view: red critical, orange serious, amber warning, green healthy, gray no data. The dot and colored edge use the same assessment. The dot does not show sampler activity.

Example

An orange dot means a serious finding, even when the sampler is sending data.

How to read it

Point at a problem tile, or move keyboard focus to it, for up to four findings with details and the process PID. Open the tile for all findings, CPU, memory, thread counts, update times, access limits, and sampler throttle status.

Measurement limits

Tiles do not run trend rules for thread growth, thread churn, or long futex waits, or memory-map layout rules. The dashboard can show more findings. A focused tile keeps its last values until focus leaves and the next refresh runs.

Source

The name and status come from the target list and latest live view. Findings use the same rules as the Assessment card. The process dashboard shows the measurements and monitoring details.

Comfortable uses larger tiles and gaps. Compact uses smaller tiles, gaps, and padding with the same text and controls. Your selection is saved in this browser. The number of targets and the 5-second refresh never change it.

observations.help:
METRIC GUIDE
Close ×
Find targets

This browser tab · Targets overview

Search shows the tiles whose process name, host, or target ID contains the text. Status shows the tiles at one assessment level, or Needs attention for critical, serious, and warning.

Example

Search db with Status Critical shows only critical targets whose name, host, or ID contains db.

How to read it

Showing N of M targets counts the tiles that match out of every monitored target. The count pills always total all targets. Clear filters shows every tile again. The page address keeps the search and status, and target links carry them, so a copied link, browser Back, and All targets on a target dashboard return to the same view. Add target stays available when no tile matches.

Measurement limits

Search and status only show or hide tiles: they start no request and do not change monitoring. A tile with keyboard focus keeps its last level until focus leaves it, so it can stay shown or hidden until the next refresh.

The collector turns counters into rates, stores history, and serves this page through /api/… endpoints. This page computes load, assessments, and findings. The optional eBPF observer adds socket bytes and messages. The Source section of each topic names its file.

Targets overview

Every target of this collector · latest live view

The first page: one tile per monitored process, with its current assessment. The counts above the tiles total every target by level, including targets that a search or status hides.

Example

Critical 1 · Healthy 3 means one process needs attention now and three show no problem.

How to read it

Tiles are sorted worst first, then by host and target ID. Select a tile, or open it in a new tab, to see that process's dashboard; All targets on the dashboard returns here. The tab title starts with the number of targets at warning or worse. The page refreshes every 5 seconds while it is visible.

Measurement limits

Tiles do not run trend rules or memory-map layout rules. Each refresh reads the latest live view of every target, so a large number of targets costs more network traffic than one dashboard.

Find targets

This browser tab · Targets overview

Search shows the tiles whose process name, host, or target ID contains the text. Status shows the tiles at one assessment level, or Needs attention for critical, serious, and warning.

Example

Search db with Status Critical shows only critical targets whose name, host, or ID contains db.

How to read it

Showing N of M targets counts the tiles that match out of every monitored target. The count pills always total all targets. Clear filters shows every tile again. The page address keeps the search and status, and target links carry them, so a copied link, browser Back, and All targets on a target dashboard return to the same view. Add target stays available when no tile matches.

Measurement limits

Search and status only show or hide tiles: they start no request and do not change monitoring. A tile with keyboard focus keeps its last level until focus leaves it, so it can stay shown or hidden until the next refresh.

help: ×Thread statesSampled scheduler state and wait channelA sampled classification of what a thread is doing or waiting for.Example. Futex wait can indicate a lock, condition variable, or timed idle wait.Running is blue and Sleep is green. State colors match across the map, state mix, charts, and wait-channel bars. Other and No access have separate gray colors. Read the state together with CPU use, run delay, and the kernel wait channel. Select a state to filter the table.Limits. Samples can miss brief transitions. A wait state does not establish that the application is unhealthy.Source. `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat` field 3, and `wchan`Field 3 of `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat` is the scheduler state letter. For a sleeping thread, `/proc/PID/task/TID/wchan` names the kernel function it waits in. The collector maps R to Running, D to Kernel wait, and T or t to Stopped. Otherwise it matches the wait channel: futex; epoll, poll, or select; socket functions; pipe or eventfd; and nanosleep. An empty wait channel is No access. Check it yourself: `ps -L -o tid,stat,wchan:32,comm -p PID`.Open metric guideFutex waitKernel wait (D)State mix

pointer: ×Past assessmentsRecordings · checked periodWhat the Assessment found in the past. The dashboard reads recorded views of the process and applies the same fixed rules as the Assessment card to each one.Example. When the page opens, up to 120 recordings of the last 15 minutes are checked, one every ~8 s. “worker-3 is saturating a core” seen from 14:02:10 to 14:05:40 in 25 checked recordings is one row, and one red mark on the timeline.Rows are newest first. Each shows the worst level it reached, when it was first and last seen, its type, and how many checked recordings had it. Select a row to move the whole dashboard to its worst moment: the Assessment card then shows the same finding and the row shows its detail. Scroll to the end of the list, select Load earlier, or release the timeline at its left end to check an earlier period; each is twice as long as the one before, up to 6 hours. While live, newer recordings are added every 15 seconds.Limits. Each period checks up to 120 recordings, so older periods are checked more coarsely: a problem that starts and ends between two of them is not listed, and its first and last times are accurate only to the step. Recording gaps end a row. Each recording is judged on its own: rules that need trends kept in a live tab (thread growth, thread churn, long futex waits) and the watch rule with no thread do not run. Resident memory growth uses the stored resource samples before each recording, combined into coarser steps for long periods. The main-stack rule runs only while the recording’s memory map is still the newest one. Nothing is stored: a reload checks again. Every checked recording is downloaded, about 330 KB each with 1,000 threads.Source. Past assessments

Recordings · checked period

What the Assessment found in the past. The dashboard reads recorded views of the process and applies the same fixed rules as the Assessment card to each one.

Example. When the page opens, up to 120 recordings of the last 15 minutes are checked, one every ~8 s. “worker-3 is saturating a core” seen from 14:02:10 to 14:05:40 in 25 checked recordings is one row, and one red mark on the timeline.

Rows are newest first. Each shows the worst level it reached, when it was first and last seen, its type, and how many checked recordings had it. Select a row to move the whole dashboard to its worst moment: the Assessment card then shows the same finding and the row shows its detail. Scroll to the end of the list, select Load earlier, or release the timeline at its left end to check an earlier period; each is twice as long as the one before, up to 6 hours. While live, newer recordings are added every 15 seconds.

Limits. Each period checks up to 120 recordings, so older periods are checked more coarsely: a problem that starts and ends between two of them is not listed, and its first and last times are accurate only to the step. Recording gaps end a row. Each recording is judged on its own: rules that need trends kept in a live tab (thread growth, thread churn, long futex waits) and the watch rule with no thread do not run. Resident memory growth uses the stored resource samples before each recording, combined into coarser steps for long periods. The main-stack rule runs only while the recording’s memory map is still the newest one. Nothing is stored: a reload checks again. Every checked recording is downloaded, about 330 KB each with 1,000 threads.

Timeline and recorded views

Selected target · collector recordings

Previous from Live opens the newest recording. Previous and Next select actual recordings. Drag to preview a time, then release to select the recording at or before it. The last selectable step returns to Live. The bar runs from the oldest time the past-assessment list has checked (at least the last 15 minutes) on the left to now on the right; coloured marks above it show when past findings were present.

Example. Select Previous to inspect the latest recorded process state. Select Live or Back to live to return to the retained live or final view.

Recorded values use the recording time and process identity. State and CPU rates come from the snapshot. Live averages, live trend charts, live socket observations, and Settings edits are unavailable. Thread history ends at the recording time. A compatible cached memory layout is labelled latest and is not a recorded layout. Release the handle at the left end to also check an earlier period, which stretches the bar further back.

Limits. A gap, missing recording, invalid reply, or read error keeps the last successful view. The collector clock can be ahead of this browser. Recording can be disabled. This Timeline does not play automatically.

recorded_at fixes the display clock. Snapshot rates cover the preceding sampling interval. Resource reads end at that time. Recordings never enter this tab's live trends or storage.

Past assessments

Recordings · checked period

What the Assessment found in the past. The dashboard reads recorded views of the process and applies the same fixed rules as the Assessment card to each one.

Example. When the page opens, up to 120 recordings of the last 15 minutes are checked, one every ~8 s. “worker-3 is saturating a core” seen from 14:02:10 to 14:05:40 in 25 checked recordings is one row, and one red mark on the timeline.

Rows are newest first. Each shows the worst level it reached, when it was first and last seen, its type, and how many checked recordings had it. Select a row to move the whole dashboard to its worst moment: the Assessment card then shows the same finding and the row shows its detail. Scroll to the end of the list, select Load earlier, or release the timeline at its left end to check an earlier period; each is twice as long as the one before, up to 6 hours. While live, newer recordings are added every 15 seconds.

Limits. Each period checks up to 120 recordings, so older periods are checked more coarsely: a problem that starts and ends between two of them is not listed, and its first and last times are accurate only to the step. Recording gaps end a row. Each recording is judged on its own: rules that need trends kept in a live tab (thread growth, thread churn, long futex waits) and the watch rule with no thread do not run. Resident memory growth uses the stored resource samples before each recording, combined into coarser steps for long periods. The main-stack rule runs only while the recording’s memory map is still the newest one. Nothing is stored: a reload checks again. Every checked recording is downloaded, about 330 KB each with 1,000 threads.

Example. 50% means 0.5 seconds of CPU time per elapsed second.

Compare CPU use with run delay. Process CPU sums all reported threads and can exceed 100%.

Limits. A high value can be normal for a busy worker. CPU use alone does not establish a problem.

Source. `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat`: utime + stime
Each sample, the sampler reads `/proc/PID/task/TID/stat` for every thread. Fields 14 (utime) and 15 (stime) are the CPU time the thread used in user and kernel mode, in clock ticks (usually 100 per second). The collector divides the change between two samples by the time between them. Process CPU sums the threads. `top -H -p PID` reads the same counters.

Recordings · checked period

What the Assessment found in the past. The dashboard reads recorded views of the process and applies the same fixed rules as the Assessment card to each one.

Example. When the page opens, up to 120 recordings of the last 15 minutes are checked, one every ~8 s. “worker-3 is saturating a core” seen from 14:02:10 to 14:05:40 in 25 checked recordings is one row, and one red mark on the timeline.

Rows are newest first. Each shows the worst level it reached, when it was first and last seen, its type, and how many checked recordings had it. Select a row to move the whole dashboard to its worst moment: the Assessment card then shows the same finding and the row shows its detail. Scroll to the end of the list, select Load earlier, or release the timeline at its left end to check an earlier period; each is twice as long as the one before, up to 6 hours. While live, newer recordings are added every 15 seconds.

Limits. Each period checks up to 120 recordings, so older periods are checked more coarsely: a problem that starts and ends between two of them is not listed, and its first and last times are accurate only to the step. Recording gaps end a row. Each recording is judged on its own: rules that need trends kept in a live tab (thread growth, thread churn, long futex waits) and the watch rule with no thread do not run. Resident memory growth uses the stored resource samples before each recording, combined into coarser steps for long periods. The main-stack rule runs only while the recording’s memory map is still the newest one. Nothing is stored: a reload checks again. Every checked recording is downloaded, about 330 KB each with 1,000 threads.

×
Process load

Process · 1-, 5-, and 15-minute averages

Smoothed demand from CPU use, runnable delay, and threads in uninterruptible kernel wait.

Example. 1.00 represents about one core of demand.

Compare the three averages to see whether demand is increasing. The chart window controls what is visible, not the averaging period.

Limits. This estimate covers the target process. It is not the host load average. Live averages need observations in this browser tab.

Source. Computed in this page from thread CPU, run delay, and kernel waits
This page computes it from each live update: the CPU use and run delay of all threads (from `stat` and `schedstat`), plus the number of threads in uninterruptible kernel wait (state D in `stat`). It applies the same exponential averaging that the kernel uses for `/proc/loadavg`, but only to this process.

Resident memory (RSS) is physical memory held by the process. Virtual size (VmSize) is its mapped address space.

invalid_or_interrupted_attempts.reason: Early help probes waited less than the documented 3000 ms. A pause-rate probe hit an existing overlay. These are invalid harness attempts.

Several checks did not await Historical/Live or used a recording without layout. Process-name fixtures became ambiguous because exited container children remained zombies. A hidden current-configuration change was wrongly included in a whole-page equality assertion. These checks are invalid; PID-owned fixtures and explicit observation waits replace them.

Immediate reads during Process details fold animation returned empty text. Some later native steps were interrupted before their deleted/long-argument fixture started. The valid first bar hover failure remains FAILED.

An unchanged prefix left Save disabled. The initial replacement history was not yet fetched. One text assertion assumed cell whitespace. Scrolling exhausted earlier periods before an outage probe. A broad help locator matched multiple cards. These are invalid setup/assertion attempts; corrected independent checks are in closing-observations.json.

The target at this point was a normal process: exe_deleted=false and command_truncated=false. This cannot test deleted/truncated details. The actual sampler pause retained valid CPU rates, so the missing-rate precondition was absent.

The diagnostic truncatedMarked flag searched for the word truncated. The requirement says marked; visible text ends with an ellipsis and the real API command_truncated flag is true. The diagnostic assertion is invalid; the observed ellipsis satisfies the c16 requirement.
The final memory reset probe used an incomplete controlled layout and failed before execution. The full-layout proof is in memory-controls-observations.json.

constraints: No product/repository edits, commits, pull requests, messages, or source build.
Only two owned qa-ui-* targets were added; both were removed.
Existing default PID38, second PID37, periodic PID63627, main collector PID267337, and sampler PID74 were preserved.
The periodic-stop file and existing watch configuration were not changed.
No native confirmation was required by the executed test-owned fixture updates. No auto-dismissed confirmation was used as evidence.

result.body:
Triangulator wire formats

The sampler and an optional socket sampler send binary datagrams over UDP to the collector. Every datagram starts with a 4-byte magic that identifies the format. Large samples are split into parts (chunks) that share sample identifiers and are put back together by the collector. Source of truth: common/wire.hpp, common/resource_wire.hpp, common/memory_wire.hpp, socket_sampler/protocol.hpp.

1. Big picture
2. Byte layouts
3. Encode / decode
4. How the pieces fit

Hover a datagram for its size, and click one in flight to drop it. Raise packet loss to watch a sample arrive incomplete. TMON uses received threads. TRES needs its summary. TVMA keeps the previous layout until all region parts arrive. TSIO stores each datagram separately. Demo timings are illustrative (real defaults: TMON every interval, TRES every 2 s, TVMA every 30 s).

completionObservations.title: Separate workers, one collector
completionObservations.caption: DashboardServer accepts connections on its own thread and starts bounded connection workers. It shares published JSON with the main receive loop. Live requests use SharedState; history requests read stored data.
completionObservations.code:
main loop: UDP → metrics → JSON
HTTP workers: request → payload
SharedState: immutable snapshots

nodes.text: Main receive loopIngest → MonitorPublish JSON every ~0.5 s

completionObservations.title: Build the page into the binary
completionObservations.caption: Vite builds dashboard/src into one HTML file. The Makefile converts that output to a byte include. http.hpp places those bytes in kDashboardHtml. The running server needs no separate dashboard file.

completionObservations.title: Start the HTTP workers
completionObservations.caption: main.cpp binds a TCP listener from the configured host and port. Listen() sets a backlog of 128. DashboardServer::Start() starts the listener thread and the socket report worker. Connection workers start as requests arrive.

completionObservations.title: Accept and parse a request
completionObservations.caption: Serve() polls the listener with a 200 ms timeout, then calls accept4(). Handle() uses ReadRequest() to read the method, path, query, and headers. Each connection has receive and send timeouts.
completionObservations.code:
poll() → accept4()
  → Handle(connection)
  → ReadRequest(connection)

GET / HTTP/1.1

completionObservations.title: Return the dashboard page
completionObservations.caption: Get() matches the root path and passes kDashboardHtml to Respond(). The browser receives HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It can now display the dashboard and request JSON.

completionObservations.title: Publish a live JSON snapshot
completionObservations.caption: The main loop builds live JSON on an approximately 500 ms refresh cycle. SetLive() exchanges a shared pointer under a mutex. SetMemoryMap() publishes a layout when its version changes.

help.name: Explain complete-sample latency
help.text:
Complete-sample latency

The sampler takes a timestamp at the start of a thread tick. Latency ends at the last thread packet’s kernel arrival on loopback. It includes thread discovery, /proc reads, encoding, and UDP. It excludes receiver scheduling and collector work. For 500 threads at 10 Hz: median 4.077 ms; p95 4.372 ms.

p95 means 95% of the measured samples completed within that time. This benchmark uses one busy thread and sleeping workers. It does not measure an application with every thread busy.

p95 means 95% of the measured samples completed within that time. This benchmark uses one busy thread and sleeping workers. It does not measure an application with every thread busy.

help.name: Explain throughput chart
help.text:
Delivered thread records

One complete sample has one record for each target thread. The measured sample frequency comes from monotonic tick timestamps. 500 threads × 10.000 observed Hz = 5,000.0 records per second.

The sampler uses the configured rate limit. These values do not measure its maximum processing capacity.

help.name: Explain frequency grid
help.text:
Frequency and thread count

Each cell is a measured count/frequency pair. Select a cell to update the cards, selected chart series, and sample interval. Latency uses the median of all samples. CPU uses the mean across 3 trials.

Brighter cells show higher values within the chosen metric. The cell text gives the value without relying on color.

help.name: Explain sample interval share
help.text:
Share of the sample interval

At 10 Hz, sample starts are 100 ms apart. A p95 latency of 4.372 ms uses 4.37% of that interval.

This is wall latency, not CPU use or a maximum sustainable rate. Auxiliary sampling takes additional time after the thread packets are sent.

Close

help.name: Explain sampler CPU
help.text:
Sampler CPU

CPU is execution time from /proc/PID/schedstat divided by monotonic elapsed time. 100% equals one core. The sampler used 4.113% of one core for 500 threads at 10 Hz.

This mean includes default resource and memory-map work. The target workload’s CPU use and the receiver’s CPU use are separate.

Close

help.name: Explain resident memory
help.text:
Resident set size

RSS is the sampler’s resident process memory from /proc/PID/smaps_rollup. Mean 2.03 MiB; maximum observed 2.03 MiB. The driver reads it each second and at the end of each trial.

RSS excludes kernel allocations, target memory, and receiver memory. Short peaks between observations can be missed.

help.text:
How the results are combined

The selected case has 900 complete samples across 3 trials. p50 is the pooled median; p95 uses nearest rank. Trial medians range from 4.066 to 4.092 ms. CPU, RSS, and throughput use the mean across trials.

These are observed values, not confidence intervals or latency guarantees. Low-frequency cases have fewer samples. Raw JSON includes every latency observation and per-trial metrics.

offlineObservations.title: Sampler performance lab — Triangulator
method:
Sampling-loop method and evidence

The timed batch calls FindTarget, Rescan, and TakeSample, then retains each complete thread record. It reuses cached file descriptors. CLOCK_MONOTONIC measures each batch. The loop has no sampling-frequency limit. Percentiles use nearest rank across all 3 repeats.

The continuous loop has different cache and scheduling conditions from the frequency-controlled sampler. The difference between these latency values and UDP delivery latency cannot be attributed to UDP alone. These values do not establish full sampler or collector capacity.

make benchmark-sampling

Recorded sampling-loop baseline · Timed C++ path · Driver

Metric definitions and measurement limits
Complete-sample latency

The sampler writes a real-time timestamp at the start of a thread tick. The receiver uses SO_TIMESTAMPNS_NEW to get each UDP packet’s kernel arrival time. Latency is the latest arrival across all chunks minus that tick timestamp. It includes thread discovery, /proc reads, packet encoding, and loopback UDP. It excludes receiver scheduling, JSON decoding, collector processing, disk writes, and resource or memory-map work after thread delivery. See the Linux timestamp documentation.

Percentiles and repeat variation

p50 is the median of all measured samples for a case. p95 is the nearest-rank 95th percentile of the same observations. Max is the slowest observed sample. The low-frequency cases have fewer observations. A p95 value is a measured tail statistic, not a latency guarantee or confidence interval. The help button next to the table shows the median range across trials for the selected case.

Delivered throughput

Thread records per second equals thread count × observed complete-sample frequency. Frequency uses the elapsed monotonic time between the first and last measured tick. A complete sample contains every expected target thread ID exactly once. This is delivered throughput at 1–10 Hz. The benchmark does not run the sampler without a rate limit, so it cannot establish saturation capacity.

CPU and resident memory

CPU uses the change in /proc/PID/schedstat execution time divided by monotonic elapsed time. 100% means one CPU core. RSS comes from /proc/PID/smaps_rollup, read once per second and at the end. MiB = 1,048,576 bytes. RSS excludes kernel allocations. CPU includes the default resource and memory-map sampling; thread-delivery latency ends before that work.

Scope and environment

These results apply to this host, build, and workload. The host runs a normal desktop; CPUs are not isolated and frequency is not fixed. Most target threads sleep. Results do not establish overhead for 500 CPU-bound threads, rapid thread creation, another host, a remote network, or the collector. Kernel arrival timestamps avoid receiver scheduling delay, but the receiver and desktop can still compete for host resources.

Loss and clock checks

The driver verifies all chunks, packet signatures, session continuity, exact target thread IDs, tick sequence, and tick spacing. It reads one complete sample beyond each measurement window to check the trailing boundary. A missing tick, incomplete sample, warning, or invalid clock measurement aborts the run. Real-time and monotonic elapsed times must agree within 0.1 ms across each run.

Source, build, and evidence

Sampler code is unchanged from the version measured by the sampling-loop benchmark. The benchmark driver adds thread-count coverage, latency timestamps, and checks across measurement boundaries.

Separate workers, one collector

DashboardServer accepts connections on its own thread and starts bounded connection workers. It shares published JSON with the main receive loop. Live requests use SharedState; history requests read stored data.

Why the threads are separate

The main loop receives UDP samples. The HTTP workers can wait on a browser or a history query without doing that work in the receive loop.

A mutex protects the snapshot pointer exchange. Each HTTP worker retains an immutable JSON string and sends it after the lock is released.

Connection limits

Serve() starts up to 64 connection workers. A slow request uses one worker. The listener backlog is 128. Reading the complete request has a 5-second total deadline. Sending the response has a separate 5-second total deadline. Excess connections receive HTTP 503.

Responses use HTTP/1.0. The connection closes after each request. The C++ server uses plain HTTP and has no TLS handshake.

Separate workers, one collector

DashboardServer accepts connections on its own thread and starts bounded connection workers. It shares published JSON with the main receive loop. Live requests use SharedState; history requests read stored data.

HTTP workers: request → payload

Why the threads are separate

The main loop receives UDP samples. The HTTP workers can wait on a browser or a history query without doing that work in the receive loop.

A mutex protects the snapshot pointer exchange. Each HTTP worker retains an immutable JSON string and sends it after the lock is released.

Connection limits

Serve() starts up to 64 connection workers. A slow request uses one worker. The listener backlog is 128. Reading the complete request has a 5-second total deadline. Sending the response has a separate 5-second total deadline. Excess connections receive HTTP 503.

Responses use HTTP/1.0. The connection closes after each request. The C++ server uses plain HTTP and has no TLS handshake.

The measured sample frequency comes from monotonic tick timestamps. 500 threads × 10.000 observed Hz = 5,000.0 records per second. The sampler uses the configured rate limit. These values do not measure its maximum processing capacity. Close

Help: Frequency and thread count Each cell is a measured count/frequency pair. Select a cell to update the cards, selected chart series, and sample interval. Latency uses the median of all samples. Help: Share of the sample interval At 10 Hz, sample starts are 100 ms apart. A p95 latency of 4.372 ms uses 4.37% of that interval. This is wall latency, not CPU use or a maximum sustainable rate. Auxiliary sampling takes additional time after the thread packets are sent. Close

Help: Sampler CPU CPU is execution time from /proc/PID/schedstat divided by monotonic elapsed time. 100% equals one core. The sampler used 4.113% of one core for 500 threads at 10 Hz. This mean includes default resource and memory-map work. The target workload’s CPU use and the receiver’s CPU use are separate. Close

Help: Resident set size RSS is the sampler’s resident process memory from /proc/PID/smaps_rollup. Mean 2.03 MiB; maximum observed 2.03 MiB. The driver reads it each second and at the end of each trial. RSS excludes kernel allocations, target memory, and receiver memory. Short peaks between observations can be missed. Close

Help: How the results are combined The selected case has 900 complete samples across 3 trials. p50 is the pooled median; p95 uses nearest rank. Trial medians range from 4.066 to 4.092 ms. QA-021.title: Separate workers, one collector
QA-021.caption: DashboardServer accepts connections on its own thread and starts bounded connection workers. It shares published JSON with the main receive loop. Live requests use SharedState; history requests read stored data.
QA-021.code:
main loop: UDP → metrics → JSON
HTTP workers: request → payload
SharedState: immutable snapshots

nodes.text: Main receive loopIngest → MonitorPublish JSON every ~0.5 s

QA-021.title: Build the page into the binary
QA-021.caption: Vite builds dashboard/src into one HTML file. The Makefile converts that output to a byte include. http.hpp places those bytes in kDashboardHtml. The running server needs no separate dashboard file.
QA-021.code:
dashboard/src
  → dashboard/dist/index.html
  → build/dashboard_html.inc
  → kDashboardHtml[]
  → triangulator-collector

QA-021.title: Start the HTTP workers
QA-021.caption: main.cpp binds a TCP listener from the configured host and port. Listen() sets a backlog of 128. DashboardServer::Start() starts the listener thread and the socket report worker. Connection workers start as requests arrive.

QA-021.title: Accept and parse a request
QA-021.caption: Serve() polls the listener with a 200 ms timeout, then calls accept4(). Handle() uses ReadRequest() to read the method, path, query, and headers. Each connection has receive and send timeouts.
QA-021.code:
poll() → accept4()
  → Handle(connection)
  → ReadRequest(connection)

GET / HTTP/1.1

QA-021.title: Return the dashboard page
QA-021.caption: Get() matches the root path and passes kDashboardHtml to Respond(). The browser receives HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It can now display the dashboard and request JSON.
QA-021.code:
GET /
  → Get()
  → kDashboardHtml
  → Respond(200, …,
      "text/html; charset=utf-8")

QA-021.title: Publish a live JSON snapshot
QA-021.caption: The main loop builds live JSON on an approximately 500 ms refresh cycle. SetLive() exchanges a shared pointer under a mutex. SetMemoryMap() publishes a layout when its version changes.
QA-021.code:
DumpJson(live)
  → shared_ptr<const string>
  → state.SetLive(…)

Layout changed? SetMemoryMap(…)

QA-021.title: Fetch JSON and update the charts
QA-021.caption: The dashboard fetches /api/live, then schedules the next refresh after 1 second. Get() reads SharedState::Live(). It sends the saved JSON without querying SQLite. Browser JavaScript updates the charts.
QA-021.code:
fetch("/api/live")
  → state_.Live()
  → Respond(200, JSON,
      "application/json")
  → browser renders metrics

QA-021.caption: The thread history request supplies a session, TID, and time range. History() validates these values and reads SQLite day files. The response contains rows, limit, and truncated fields.

QA-021.title: Send bytes, then close
QA-021.caption: Respond() adds HTTP/1.0 headers and sends until all bytes are written or send() fails. FileDescriptor closes the connection when its scope ends. Serve() then waits for the next connection.

help.name: Explain complete-sample latency
help.text:
Complete-sample latency

The sampler takes a timestamp at the start of a thread tick. Latency ends at the last thread packet’s kernel arrival on loopback. It includes thread discovery, /proc reads, encoding, and UDP. It excludes receiver scheduling and collector work. For 500 threads at 10 Hz: median 4.077 ms; p95 4.372 ms.

p95 means 95% of the measured samples completed within that time. This benchmark uses one busy thread and sleeping workers. It does not measure an application with every thread busy.

Close
